utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-47-A, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. May I ask Mr. Hadzihasanovic and Mr. Kubura if they can hear me and follow the proceedings through the translation. THE APPELLANT HADZIHASANOVIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all in the courtroom. I can hear properly and I understand everything. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hadzihasanovic. Mr. Kubura. THE APPELLANT KUBURA: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can hear you and I can understand the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Now may I ask for the appearances for Mr. Kubura first.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Mr. Kubura, Mulalic Nermin, Rodney Dixon, and my name is Fahrudin Ibrisimovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. For Mr. Hadzihasanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic and -- as lead counsel, and Stephane Bourgon as co-counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. May I turn to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCCALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, my name and Shelagh McCall. The counsel with me are Steffen Wirth, Barbara Goy and Marwan Dalal, assisted by our case manager, Sebastiaan van Hooydonk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, this is the appeal hearing in the case of the Prosecutor against Hadzihasanovic and Kubura. At the outset, I will briefly summarise the appeals which are pending for the Appeals Chamber and the manner in which we will proceed today. The appeals deal with the superior responsibility of Mr. Hadzihasanovic and Mr. Kubura for their failure to prevent or punish the crimes of units subordinated to them committed in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993. Enver Hadzihasanovic, Amir Kubura, and the Prosecution appeal from a judgement rendered on 15 March 2006 by Trial Chamber II, composed of Judge Antonetti, presiding, and Judges Rasoazanany and Swart. The Trial Chamber found General Hadzihasanovic guilty pursuant to Article 3 of the Statute for having failed to prevent or punish the offences of murder committed by his subordinates in Bugojno and at the Orasac camp, count 3; and cruel treatment committed by his subordinates at the Zenica music school, at the Orasac camp, and at the various detention centres in Bugojno, count 4. The Trial Chamber acquitted Hadzihasanovic on all other counts. The Trial Chamber sentenced Hadzihasanovic to a single term of five years imprisonment. Hadzihasanovic seeks the reversal of the convictions against him. The Prosecution appeals against -- appeals against the sentence imposed on Hadzihasanovic. The Trial Chamber found Kubura guilty pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute for having failed to prevent or punish plundering, committed by his subordinates in Vares and in the villages of the Ovnak area, count 6. The Trial Chamber acquitted Kubura on all other counts. Kubura was sentenced to a single term of imprisonment of two and a half years. Kubura has appealed his conviction and sentence. The Prosecution has appealed his acquittal for the crime of wanton destruction in the town of Vares in October 1993 and the sentence. Amir Kubura and Enver Hadzihasanovic filed their Notice of Appeal respectively on 13 and 18 April 2006. On 22nd January 2007, Kubura filed his appeal brief. On 5 February 2007, Hadzihasanovic filed his brief confidentially. Together with annexes which were themselves refiled on 27 February 2007. The Prosecution filed its Notice of Appeal on 18 April 2006 and its appeal brief on 3 July 2006. I will now briefly summarise the grounds of appeal. Amir Kubura brings three grounds of appeal. In his first ground of appeal, Kubura alleges that the Trial Chamber committed errors of fact and law in convicting him for failing to take necessary and reasonable measures to punish plunder in the villages in the Ovnak area in June 1993. Under his second ground of appeal, Kubura alleges that the Trial Chamber committed errors of fact and law in convicting him for failing to take necessary or reasonable measures to prevent punish plunder in Vares in November 1993. Under his third ground of appeal, Kubura submits the Trial Chamber erred in exercising its sentencing discretion by imposing a sentence of two and a half years of imprisonment. Hadzihasanovic brings five grounds of appeal. In his first and second grounds of appeal, he alleges that the Trial Chamber committed numerous errors of law and fact which deprives him of his right to a fair trial. Under his third ground of appeal, he alleges that the Trial Chamber committed errors of fact and law by finding that he failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to punish those responsible for the murder of Mladen Havranek and the cruel treatment of six prisoners at the furniture salon of 5 August 1993, as well as to prevent similar behaviour in the other facilities in Bugojno. Under his fourth ground of appeal, Hadzihasanovic alleges that the Trial Chamber committed error of fact and law by finding that he failed in his obligation as a superior to take necessary and reasonable measures to punish the perpetrators of the infliction of physical violence at the Zenica music school and prevent similar behaviour. Under his fifth ground of appeal, Hadzihasanovic alleges that the Trial Chamber committed errors of fact and law by finding that he failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the murder of Dragan Popovic and the cruel treatment committed between 19 and 31st October 1993 by members of the El Mujahedin Detachment. The Prosecution brings four grounds of appeal. In its first and third ground, the Prosecution alleges that Hadzihasanovic and Kubura's sentences respectively are manifestly inadequate. Under its second ground of appeal, the Prosecution appeals Kubura's acquittal under count 5 regarding the crime of wanton destruction in Vares in October 1993. And finally, under its fourth ground of appeal, the Prosecution alleges that the Trial Chamber committed an error of law by finding that the superior's duty to punish could be discharged by summary disciplinary measures. Although it concedes that this error would not have an impact on the verdict, the Prosecution raises it as an issue of general significance to the jurisprudence of the International Tribunal. Now, during this appeal briefing, counsel may argue the grounds of appeal in the order they consider most suitable for their presentation, but I would urge them not just to repeat verbatim or to extensively summarise what is in their brief which is -- have been read by the Court. I wish also to note that pursuant to the Scheduling Order of 14 November 2007, the Appeals Chamber has invited the parties to address specific issues during this appeal hearing, issues that I do not have to be -- to restate now. These invitations are made - I want to stress that - without prejudice to any matter the parties or the Appeals Chamber may wish to raise and in no way constitute an expression of the opinion on the merits of the appeal. I would now like to recall the criteria applicable to errors of fact and law alleged on appeal. The appeal is not a trial de novo and the appellants must not merely repeat their case from the trial level. Rather, in accordance with the Article 25 of the Statute, the appellants must limit their arguments to alleged errors of law which invalidate the trial judgement or alleged errors of fact, occasioning a miscarriage of justice. Additionally, it should be recalled that the appellants have an obligation to provide precise references to materials supporting their arguments on appeal. The hearing will proceed according with the schedule outlined in the decision on Hadzihasanovic expedited motion seeking admission in the record an Appeal of certain official translations and request for additional time during the appeal hearing, filed on 30 November 2007. Counsel for Kubura will present his submissions this morning for 40 minutes. The Prosecution will then present its response for 40 minutes, after which counsel for Kubura will reply for 20 minutes. Then following a pause, the Prosecution will start its appeal, according to the schedule. It will be most helpful if -- to the Appeal Chamber if the parties could present their submissions in a precise and clear manner. I wish to remind the parties that the Judges may interrupt them at any time to ask questions or they may prefer to ask questions following each party's submission. Having said that, about the manner in which we'll proceed today, I will now like to invite counsel for Mr. Kubura to present submissions in support of his appeal. Please, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I will address you only on grounds 1 and 2 of Mr. Kubura's appeal, that is, his appeal against his sole two convictions for failing to prevent and/or punish looting pursuant to Article 7(3). In respect of -- of his appeal against sentence, the appellant rests on the written submissions that have already been filed. By way of background, Mr. Kubura was granted early release by the order of the President of 11 April 2006, having served over 95 per cent of his sentence of two and a half years of imprisonment. It follows therefore that any possible reduction in sentence would be a matter purely for the record and of potential value as -- as precedent in the sentencing practices of -- of the ICTY. However, even though Mr. Kubura enjoys his freedom, his appeal against the only two convictions is, in our submission, more than purely academic. At the outset, it must be emphasized that, as far as it concerns Mr. Kubura, the appellant's submission is that the Trial Chamber's judgement as a whole is a careful and well-reasoned one. Indeed, the vast bulk of the Trial Chamber's extensive findings and acquittals, and the reasoning underpinning them, are not disputed by -- by either the Prosecution or Mr. Kubura. The appellant only submits that there were particular and confined errors in the final two findings of the Trial Chamber in respect of the sole convictions that were entered for looting for the last charges on the indictment against Mr. Kubura in count 6. These have been appealed on account of those errors both for the record and because it is, of course, a consequence of these convictions by an international court that they have an adverse effect on Mr. Kubura's future career prospects in the military of Bosnia, on alternative career opportunities, on his ability to travel, and his reputation. Lastly, by way of introduction, in the appellant's submission there is certainly no proper basis to increase Mr. Kubura's sentence, as sought by the Prosecution in its appeal at ground 3, given the -- the nature of the property-related crimes, the mitigating factors, and also taking into account the -- the detrimental consequences of the two convictions to which I have already referred. I will further briefly address Your Honours on this ground of the Prosecution's appeal at -- at the appropriate time in the schedule. Turning then to Mr. Kubura's two grounds of appeal against conviction. The appellant's only submission is that no reasonable Trial Chamber could convict Mr. Kubura on the evidence at trial for failing to punish looting in respect of Ovnak in June 1993 and for failing to prevent and punish looting later in Vares at the beginning of November 1993. In fact, on -- on one day, the 4th of November, 1993. The appellant's argument divides into three parts. And I'll go through each in sequence. Firstly, in respect of Ovnak. The appellant's key submission is that there is no evidence of Mr. Kubura possessing the requisite knowledge of unlawful appropriation of goods committed by members of his brigade, the 7th Brigade, those being his subordinates, upon which a reasonable Trial Chamber could base a conviction. The reasons are, firstly, there is no direct evidence of Mr. Kubura witnessing any plundering or any goods that had been plundered or of distributing any of these goods. The Trial Chamber pointed to no such evidence, and nor has the Prosecution referred to such evidence on the record. Secondly, there are no reports from commanders or -- or members of Mr. Kubura's brigade of plundering which came to him or to his command, or, for that matter, reports from other brigades that were involved. There are only general orders from the 3rd Corps command to all brigades -- and the word "all" is used in the orders -- to prevent plundering following operations, and these are unspecified, between the Bosnian army and the HVO. There's no specific mention of the Ovnak area in any of those orders. And here, Your Honour, I'm referring to P186, that is, the order of 10 June; and DH65, that is, the -- the order of 19 June. Mr. Kubura merely replicated those orders in passing them on to his brigade in an order to which the OTP refers of 20 June, which is P427, as did all other brigade commanders in the 3rd Corps, as they were required to do. That order of 20 June also does not specifically mention plunder in the Ovnak area or that the 7th Brigade was involved in any of those activities. And in our submission, these orders, which the Prosecution relies upon, are -- are merely evidence of Mr. Kubura obeying orders from above and passing them on, general orders from above about prevention of plundering in general and passing them on to his subordinates, as other brigades were doing. It must be emphasized, Your Honours, in this context that the Trial Chamber found - and this is at paragraph 1943 - that various brigades, refugees, and civilians were involved in the plunder in the Ovnak area. So, Your Honours, we -- we are then left with what the Trial Chamber clearly based its findings on, which is the -- the key paragraph in this regard, paragraph 1957, and there the Trial Chamber based its finding of knowledge for Mr. Kubura on the evidence of one witness, Witness BA, who said that plundered property from Ovnak was distributed by the 7th Brigade, and the Trial Chamber reasoned that that process must have required a decision from the command and, therefore, Mr. Kubura. Yet, the evidence of Witness BA is that he did not know by whom and how that distribution process was performed. That's at transcript reference 808 to 809. And there is no other evidence on the record of that distribution process; it comes solely from that one witness. Moreover, the Trial Chamber did find explicitly that Mr. Kubura's presence in the headquarters where the goods were apparently distributed was not established beyond reasonable doubt. And that's paragraph 1956. The Trial Chamber also found that the army had the right to seize private property that could be used directly for military purposes. That's at paragraph 1941. There was thus nothing improper about setting up collection points for such property, termed "war booty," or setting up commissions to deal with that, as was ordered by Mr. Kubura in his order of 5 June 1993. That's P420 and referred to at -- at paragraph 1939. So in our submission, it's not correct, as the Prosecution suggest, that those orders show that he knew about property that had been plundered. They merely show that he was implementing a lawful system that was accepted by the Trial Chamber as such within his brigade. There are, we submit - and this is the crucial point - no orders concerning the distribution of any goods that were obtained from Ovnak and no reports to Mr. Kubura that he knew about that process. Indeed, as I have underlined, Witness BA was not able to give any evidence about who was involved in that process. Moving on, then, Your Honours, to the second part of the argument. And -- and that is whether there are any other instances of plunder from June 1993, Ovnak, until November 1993, in Vares. The Prosecution was requested by Your Honours to identify evidence of plunder committed by the 7th Brigade between those two months. And in the Defence's submission, there is no such evidence of particular instances for which Mr. Kubura could be held responsible under Article 7(3) for failing to prevent or punish plunder. He certainly was -- was not charged with any other incidents on -- on the evidence. There is, thus, no evidence of a repetitive pattern which Mr. Kubura failed to prevent and which could have put him on notice or from which it can be concluded that he should have anticipated further unlawful acts. As I've already submitted, there is, in our submission, no evidence in respect of Ovnak about him having knowledge of his troops' involvement. But -- but even assuming such -- such knowledge, in our submission, there's no evidence of any continuing transgressions thereafter, and it is for the OTP to prove knowledge of plunder in Vares in early November in order to be able to hold Mr. Kubura responsible for failing to prevent it. The -- the final part of my submission in respect of the grounds of appeal relates to -- to Vares. So we've now moved to the final segment of the conduct. As with Ovnak, in our submission, there's no evidence that Mr. Kubura possessed the requisite knowledge of any particular offences of plunder committed by his subordinates in the 7th Brigade. The Trial Chamber clearly found that this operation was a multi-corps, multi-brigade operation, involving three corps, in fact, under the command of a operational group called the OG Istok. And that, Your Honours, is at paragraph 1966 and 1978. There is no evidence that Mr. Kubura witnessed any plundering in Vares on the 4th of November or at any time immediately thereafter. There's also no evidence that he received any reports from his subordinates that plundering was in fact occurring. On the contrary, Kasim Podzic, who was the commander of the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Brigade that was in Vares on the day, testified that his troops withdrew on orders at 3.00 p.m. and were not involved in looting or taking goods from Vares. That's transcript reference 18656 to 18658. And, Your Honours, for completeness, his testimony was referred to by the Trial Chamber at paragraph 1838, without making any comment on the credibility or lack thereof of -- of that witness. The Trial Chamber appears to have relied upon what the witness said in his testimony. As accepted by the Trial Chamber, in addition to -- to these shortcomings in the evidence, the two reports from the operational group command of 4 November about plunder in Vares were not sent to Mr. Kubura. That's accepted in the judgement. The two documents are P445 and P676. Consequently, on the judgement, it is plain that there are only three documents left upon which the Trial Chamber based its conclusion. That is, P675, P446, and P468. And that's at the crucial paragraph in respect of this count, paragraph 1986. The Prosecution suggests that the appellant has -- has looked at these documents artificially and in isolation without considering their property sequence and all of the surrounding evidence. On the contrary, we will place them in their full context. And in the short time remaining, Your Honours, I just wish to look at each document and show its relationship, and that will conclude my submission. Firstly, in relation to -- to P675, that is an order from the OG command of 4 November, so on the day of -- of the plunder. Your Honours will see that it's not addressed to the 7th Brigade but states that "the army" - and I'm quoting - "The army must withdraw and also must stop anything being removed from the town." The 7th Brigade commander is specifically made responsible for the execution of that order, but - and this is crucial, in our submission - there is no mention in that order of the 7th Brigade committing any acts of plunder on the 4th of November. Your Honours, I'll come back to this order when I look at what did the 7th Brigade in fact order on that day and -- and thereafter. The next document is P446. This is a report, Your Honours, from the 3rd Corps command to the OG command. It's also dated 4 November, and it states that: "We have issued orders to brigades to engage all military police in preventing looting." Now, the Trial Chamber found that -- that this must have been conveyed to the 7th Brigade, as the 7th Brigade was the only brigade of the 3rd Corps involved in Vares. In our submission, there is an initial point that is incorrect in that finding, in that the 7th Brigade was not the only brigade of the 3rd Corps involved in Vares. Document P448, which is a report on -- on the operations, makes it clear that there were many brigades of the 3rd Corps involved, and other units. And in any event, as the report states, the word "brigades," plural, is -- is used, and not just "the 7th Brigade" or "a brigade." But most importantly, it is not evidence that Mr. Kubura was informed of his particular subordinates committing acts of plunder in a multi-corps, multi-brigade operation. The last document, P468, this is a report from the 2nd Battalion to the 7th Brigade command of the 11th of November, so some days later. In our submission, it is not evidence from which it is capable to conclude from unlawful acts were committed by subordinates of Mr. Kubura in particular. It only mentions the appropriation of war booty according to the lawful policy, to which I referred earlier, Your Honours, and it states in terms that looting was prevented. In our submission, that therefore could not be evidence that looting occurred if the report is that it has not. Your Honours have -- have asked the parties the question: When on the evidence did Mr. Kubura know about looting in Vares on the 4th of November? The answer, in our submission, on the evidence is that at no time did he learn that his subordinates in particular were involved in looting on 4 November. The Trial Chamber pointed to two orders of -- of the 7th Brigade, as do the -- the Prosecution. That's DK50 and P478. Now, these are both orders from the 7th Brigade. One of the -- the 4th of November and the next of the 5th of November. But neither of these orders mention that the 7th Brigade is to withdraw on account of plunder committed by the 7th Brigade or of receiving any order to withdraw on account of any plunder committed by members of the 7th Brigade. Your Honours, in our submission, what these orders represent is, as I mentioned earlier -- I would refer back to P675, which was the order of the OG command for the army to withdraw. Well, what these orders represent is the 7th Brigade being ordered by its command to withdraw its troops on the 4th of November, as all forces were ordered to do in this multi-brigade operation. In summary, these documents are not evidence of knowledge of plunder committed by members of the 7th Brigade, but they are evidence only of the 7th Brigade following orders from above to withdraw, as all subordinate brigades involved in that operation were required to do. Your Honours, in conclusion, I refer briefly to the -- the jurisprudence at -- at paragraph 12 of the appellant's appeal brief. I don't wish to go through it in detail, given the -- the time constraints, and it is set out clearly in -- in our brief. But it is to the effect that knowledge cannot be presumed. This is knowledge, direct, constructive, or having reason to know. The burden is on the Prosecution to prove by reference to information which is in fact available to the superior, not on information that could be presumed to be available to him. That information has to be shown to have come from reports or orders or meetings or from witnesses directly. In the appellant's submission, the -- the knowledge requirement of Article 7(3) has not been established on the actual information that was available to Mr. Kubura at the time, and therefore we say that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have convicted on the basis of that available evidence. Those are my submissions. Of course, we incorporate all of our written submissions. These were just the main points that were highlighted. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you,. Judge Liu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel, I'm very interested in the frequency and the scope of the 7th Brigade military operations during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That is, from June to November of that year. Will you please be kind enough to identify the evidence in the trial records, as well as the portions of the trial judgement concerning of those military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, thank you. This was a matter in fact that I had discussed with the -- the Prosecution, because the -- the question was initially posed to the Prosecution as to what evidence they would rely upon to show operations during that time and if there were any particular incidents of -- of plunder. In our examination of -- of the record, there -- there was no evidence presented of any further operations of the 7th Brigade during that time. That's not to say that they weren't involved in such operations. In fact, P621, which is a document that my learned friend from the Prosecution may -- may refer to, indicates that there were numerous other operations involving the 7th Brigade and other brigades, of course, of the 3rd Corps during that time. But as there were no charges specific to Mr. Kubura for those operations, there was no further evidence led in -- in respect of them. Your Honour, perhaps the most important question, though, is: Is there any evidence of plunder committed during that time period? I know my learned friend from the Prosecution is going to address Your Honours on this point, and I was proposing to reply thereafter. But I can say at this point that, in our submission, there are no other instances that Mr. Kubura could have been held responsible for; in other words, having known about it and having failed to prevent or punish, of plunder committed by members of the 7th Brigade during that time. There is evidence of certain punitive measures and disciplinary measures being taken against members of the 7th Brigade to which my learned friend may refer, but in our submission, those are outside of a military context. They involve robberies and the theft of a car in towns, and they're not -- they're not offences that arose as part of military operations for which Mr. Kubura could have been held responsible for failing to act, if indeed that had been the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Guney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does Mr. Kubura have the requisite knowledge [In English] sufficient to trigger a duty to prevent his subordinates from committing further acts of plunder in Vares as of his receipt of the orders alerting him to these ongoing acts, but did satisfy his duty to prevent the plunder by putting a stop at the plunder once it had started so it would not be repeated? This is the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the -- the relevant orders of the two that I referred to - that's P478 and DK50, which is Mr. Kubura ordering his troops to withdraw immediately - and in respect of those, our submission is that they show that he did act immediately to withdraw his troops once the order came from above that the army must immediately get out of Vares. But they are not evidence that he did that because he knew that his subordinates were committing acts of plunder. There may well have been genuine information about a multi-corps, multi-brigade involvement in acts of plunder, but in our submission, that's -- that -- that's not sufficient. He needs to be put on notice that his troops were committing acts and that, as a result of that, he was required to take certain action. But in our submission, he cannot be criticised for not following orders from above. His troops were immediately withdrawn. And there's also evidence that there was a check-point checking them as they were coming out. That's the evidence of Mr. Podzic, which is referred to in our appeal brief. So, Your Honour, if I've understood your question correctly, yes, on the 4th of November he did withdraw his troops, but we say that there's no evidence he had knowledge that his troops had committed unlawful acts and that therefore he withdrew them on -- on that day. That's the gist of our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Guney. Sorry, Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel, if Kubura knew nevertheless of the plundering in the Ovnak area in June 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- does that knowledge mean or does not necessarily mean that he knew or had reason to know about the plunder that occurred in Vares in November 1993? And related to that, do I understand you to say that there was no other evidence of his knowledge or constructive knowledge of the plundering in Vares?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, if I could start with the first question. In -- in our submission, the mere fact, if it is established that he did know in June of plunder in Vares, it's not in and of itself sufficient to hold him responsible for failing to prevent or -- or know about acts that are to come in November. The evidence is of plunder on a single day in Ovnak and then a single day in -- in November in Vares, with some five months between. And in our submission, unless there's evidence of a repetitive pattern which would put him on notice over a period of time, it would be stretching it to say that he -- because he knew in June, therefore he must have known later. That's in respect of the first question. In respect of the second, we -- we say there is no evidence that he knew that his troops were committing acts of plunder in Vares in -- in 1993. There are the orders that circulated about looting and burning, but those -- as the Trial Chamber found, were going between the OG command and the 3rd Corps command and back. There are no orders in evidence that -- that go from the 3rd Corps command to the 7th Brigade. There is the one order which I referred to, P675, saying the 7th Brigade is responsible for implementing this order, but that's not an order to stop the 7th Brigade members from committing any acts of -- of plunder. It's an order to withdraw and to stop goods being removed when they do withdraw. And in our submission, as -- as I said, that process did occur; Mr. Kubura can't be faulted in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: There are no other questions. I would invite the Prosecution to respond to the appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Steffen Wirth. I will be stressing you -- addressing you on the first two grounds of appeal of Amir Kubura. Like the Defence for Amir Kubura, we do not propose to address Kubura's third ground of appeal, his appeal against the sentence, and in that regard we rely upon our brief. In any event, the Chamber will be aware that the Prosecution will be addressing Mr. Kubura -- the sentence of Mr. Kubura in its own appeal in due course. I turn to Mr. Kubura's first ground, regarding the plunder of Ovnak, of the Ovnak area. Before I address the arguments raised this morning, I will give a short overview over the relevant factual framework of this ground of appeal. On the 8th of June, 1993, the 7th Brigade entered the Ovnak area from which the Croatian troops had already withdrawn. On the following day, the 9th of June, 1993, the members of the 7th Brigade and others committed extensive and repeated plunder in the area. Many houses were plundered, technical equipment -- many houses were plundered and technical equipment, valuable household appliances, and food was stolen. The plundered goods were systematically collected in the church of Brajkovici -- Brajkovcici [sic], one of the villages in the Ovnak area, and eventually transported to the Bilmiste barracks in Zenica, that is, Kubura's headquarters. Eventually the stolen goods were distributed among the members of the 7th Brigade. The Trial Chamber found that Kubura knew of the plunder and failed to take any steps to punish the perpetrators and therefore convicted him for the failure to punish plunder in Ovnak. Kubura submits that the Chamber failed -- that the Chamber erred - excuse me - the Chamber erred in finding that Kubura knew of the plunder. The Trial Chamber found that the stolen goods were distributed among members of the 7th Brigade and drew the conclusion that this distribution could not have been done without at least Mr. Kubura's consent. It has been Mr. Kubura's submission this morning that the Trial Chamber should not have drawn this conclusion and there are two arguments. The first argument is that the Trial Chamber only relied upon a single witness, Witness BA. And the second argument is that the Trial Chamber erred in drawing the conclusion that Kubura must at least have consented to the distribution of the goods. Now, both arguments should be rejected. First, the Trial Chamber was entitled to rely upon the evidence of one witness, that is found in the Aleksovski appeals judgement, paragraph 62. But second, there were several pieces of evidence, not just one, that show that the plundered goods were brought to Kubura's headquarters and that he decided about or consented to their distribution. This evidence is the following: The plundered goods were delivered directly to Kubura's headquarters, the Bilmiste barracks in Zenica. Also, it was Kubura who had chosen the Bilmiste barracks as a collection point for booty, and that is P420 and trial judgement 1939. And even if that was a lawful procedure, as has been submitted to us this morning, this procedure has been abused by using it to process not legal war booty but stolen goods. Now, it was not a secret that the goods taken from Ovnak were taken to the 7th Brigade's facilities. This fact was known to the Zenica Municipal Defence Staff Security and Information Service and the service reported the fact to the 3rd Corps command two days after the plunder of the 11th June. And that is P424, referred to in trial judgement 1936. Now, there is also evidence -- contrary to Kubura's submissions there is also evidence that show it was Kubura who decided about the distribution of goods. He did so in a meeting of 7th July, 1993. And that is P789. And he did so with regard to the goods plundered in Vares. That's found by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 1993. Finally, the organised scheme for the plunder in Ovnak could not have been implemented without prior approval of Mr. Kubura, and that is the finding of the Trial Chamber in paragraph 2091. Taken together, this evidence shows that the 7th Brigade troops systematically and extensively plundered the Ovnak area, that they openly used 7th Brigade premises at Kubura's headquarters to store the plundered goods; that this location had been designated as a collection point by Mr. Kubura; and that Mr. Kubura generally was the person to decide about the distribution of goods. Given that evidence, the Trial Chamber was not unreasonable to conclude that Kubura at least had consented to the distribution of the goods taken from Ovnak. It -- therefore, Mr. Kubura must have known of the plunder. I turn to Mr. Kubura's second ground of appeal, unless Your Honours have questions with regard to the first ground. But before I address Mr. Kubura's arguments, I will first answer the Appeals Chamber' questions with regard to this ground. I begin with question 3A, and that is whether the 7th Brigade had been engaged in military operations between June and November 1993 and whether acts of plunder were committed during such operations. The answer is that there is evidence that the 7th Brigade was engaged in military operations in this time frame and there is evidence of plunder. P621 is a request from Kubura to rest soldiers. It is dated 16 October 1993 and it states that "The 7th Brigade had been in constant combat since April and thus required 12 to 15 days of rest." Now, this is evidence that the 7th Brigade was involved in military operations in the time frame. I'll turn now to the evidence that they plundered during such operations. Now, first, around the same time, when the Ovnak area was plundered, members of the 7th Brigade committed repeated and extensive plunder in Cukle, that is trial judgement 1913 and 1915. Kubura was not charged with these incidents. That's why there's no conviction -- or that's why the Trial Chamber didn't address the conviction. That is 1926 in the trial judgement. The plunder in Cukle followed the attack on the village. That is trial judgement 1910. Now, for the next piece of evidence, I would like to refer to -- I would ask Your Honours could we go in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: This evidence is corroborated by P898, a report of the 3rd Corps which states that on 7th June 1993 a member of the MOS was involved in taking technical goods on a wagon in the Ovnak area. Now, the Trial Chamber found that the term "MOS" in this report meant the 7th Brigade. And you can see that from trial judgement paragraph 1943 in conjunction with trial judgement paragraph 410. The next piece of evidence regards the 7th Brigade's plunder in Kakanj. Two 7th Brigade members were under investigation for allegations of looting in Kakanj and several officers of the 7th Brigade were relieved of their duties by the commander of the 7th Brigade for failing to prevent the crime of looting in Kakanj. That is P544, a report from Hadzihasanovic dated 25th June 1993. Now, this document does not only show that the 7th Brigade was involved in plunder but also that Kubura knew of this and reacted by merely relieving officers of their duties. Further, plunder in Fojnica. In the Fojnica sector, 7th Brigade soldiers were combing through Croatian houses. That's P814 [Realtime transcript read in error "P840"], a report of the 7th Brigade command of the 5th of August, 1993. There are also several criminal reports on the record accusing members of the 7th Brigade of taking goods at gunpoint from their owners. Members of the 7th Brigade were reported to have used their weapons to take away a car from Davor Blazevic on the 16th of August, 1993. That is DH1481, a criminal report against members of 7th Brigade. Another criminal report, Exhibit DH1553 is directed against members of the 7th Brigade who took money and other goods from their victims, again at gunpoint, at various times from July to September 1993. The fact that the soldiers were reported to have taken the goods at gunpoint shows that they acted during military operations. ABiH soldiers only had long-barreled weapons. And that is transcript page 13768, and ABiH soldiers were only allowed to carry long-barreled weapons during military operations. That is DH2086, section viii, and that confirmed in P447, number 5. Now, in addition to this evidence of plunder carried out by members of the 7th Brigade, further documents show that plunder was a recurring problem of which the ABiH was well aware. Several orders of Hadzihasanovic addressed the problem of plunder. These orders are referred to in paragraph 2024 and following of the trial judgement. I will therefore only point out two of them today. The first one is P193, an order of the 3rd Corps command of 18 September 1993. This order strictly forbade the looting of property and required that if it takes place, commanders, including brigade commanders, must take necessary action to impose sanctions. The order was directed inter alia to all brigades. The second order that I would like to point out is the order to attack Vares. This is the order which was sent to Kubura on the 3rd of November, 1993, P674. This order, one day before the attack on Vares, explicitly re-emphasises to Kubura that war booty must be dealt with in the spirit of the 3rd Corps command order. Now, contrary to Kubura's submission this morning, these orders directed against the virulent problem of plunder, together with the evidence of the ongoing plunder by members of the 7th Brigade show that the looting of Ovnak was not an isolated incident, it was not something that Kubura could disregard when preparing for the attack on Vares. I will now turn to the Appeals Chamber question number 3B. The first part of the question is: When in the course of the 4th of November, 1993 did Kubura acquire knowledge of the plunder? Now, this is not clear from the evidence. It is known that the 7th Brigade entered the town around 8.00. Trial judgement 1966. And it is known that chaos erupted after the 7th Brigade had entered the town. That is P -- and it is also known that everything was looted at the time. P676. It is further clear that the OG Istok learned of the plunder at the latest at 10.45, when its Chief of Staff reported that the 7th Brigade had entered the town and that they were stealing everything they saw. It is also known that OG Istok, as well as the 3rd Corps command, ordered to stop the plunder. P675 and P446. But time when Kubura received these orders is not in evidence. The second part of question 3B is: How and when did Kubura react to stop the plunder? And the answer is that Kubura ordered his troops to withdraw and that this order was received at 1500 hours. That's T18657, corroborated by P448, page 12. Now, this ends my submissions on the Appeals Chamber' questions. And unless there's anything else with regard to these questions that I can assist the Appeals Chamber with I would turn to Kubura's submission on the second ground of appeal. Now, again, before I turn to Kubura's arguments, I will give a short overview of the facts of the case. On the 4th of November, when the 7th Brigade entered the abandoned town of Vares, chaos erupted and everything was looted and burned. That's P676, a report from OG Istok. The 7th Brigade soldiers were stealing and looting everything they saw, and after learning the situations, members of other units joined in the general looting. P445 and trial judgement 1955. ABiH soldiers who appeared to be drunk were going around and shooting their weapons. There were broken windows and smashed-in doors. The 7th Brigade was responsible for the wholesale smashing of shop windows, making off with goods, and smashing cars. That's P448, page 11, an analysis by OG Istok. And as counsel for the Defence just pointed out, OG Istok commanded the operation in Vares. The primary object of the plunder were shops in the main street but also private houses. Now, on the basis of this and other evidence, the Trial Chamber found that the crime of plunder had been committed by several units of the ABiH, and particularly by soldiers of the 7th Brigade 2nd and 3rd Battalions. The Trial Chamber also found Kubura's knowledge on two distinct bases: First, the Trial Chamber found that Kubura had reason to know of the upcoming plunder in Vares since he knew of the prior plunder in the Ovnak area. And I just made submissions on that matter with regard to the Appeals Chamber's questions. The second basis for Kubura's knowledge was that he learned of the actual plunder after he -- it had started, and several documents show that. That is trial judgement 1986. The Trial Chamber found that before the plunder, Kubura did not take sufficient measures to take -- to prevent the plunder from starting and that after the plunder he did not take measures to punish the perpetrators. The Trial Chamber consequently convicted Kubura for failing to prevent and punish the plunder in Vares. I will now turn to Kubura's appeal against his conviction. The Trial Chamber's first basis for finding Kubura's mens rea was that the plunder in Ovnak, combined with Kubura's failure to punish, put him on notice that the 7th Brigade was likely to repeat such acts. Kubura claims, first, that the Trial Chamber erred because Kubura had not known of the plunder in Ovnak. And I have just addressed why that is not correct. Kubura also claims - excuse me - that there was a long period of time between the plunder in Ovnak and the plunder in Vares and that the information that the warning he received in Ovnak somehow had worn off in the meantime. Now, I also have addressed that matter when addressing the Appeals Chamber's questions, showing that plunder was a very, very live issue and that Kubura was aware of that. I turn to the second basis for Kubura's mens rea, and that was that he learned of the plunder after it had started. The Trial Chamber found that Kubura learned of the plunder of his troops since he received two orders, two orders and one report notifying him of this fact. And this evidence is set out in the trial judgement in paragraph 1986. Now, the first document is P675, and that is an order by the OG Istok which requires that the plunder be stopped and assigns Mr. Kubura to carry out that order. The Trial Chamber also found that Mr. Kubura reacted to this order and that he withdrew his troops from Vares. The Defence claims that -- the Defence points out that P675 does not specifically state that the 7th Brigade was involved in the plunder; however, the fact that Mr. Kubura was assigned to carry out that order was a -- a basis for a reasonable Trial Chamber to find that he had known from this -- that he was informed through this order that his troops committed plunder in Vares. In any case, however, if nothing else, this order clearly put him on inquiry notice. It clearly indicates that -- the need for further investigations that he needs to take in order to find out who was plundering in Vares, since he certainly knew that his troops were there. Now, the second document, the second order that reached Mr. Kubura was an order of the 3rd Corps command. The Exhibit P448 reports this order and states that the order was sent to brigades. The Trial Chamber found that the 7th Brigade was the only brigade subordinated to the 3rd Corps that was present in Vares and that therefore this exhibit must have been -- sorry, that therefore this order, the order reported in P446, must have reached the 7th Brigade. Kubura has submitted this morning that P448 would mention that other brigades of the 3rd Corps were also present in Vares. I have very quickly reviewed P448 and particularly pages 11 to 12, where the Vares plunder -- where the Vares operation and the plunder is mentioned, and I was not able to find information that also other brigades of the 7th -- of the 3rd Corps were present in the Vares area. In any case, it cannot be assumed that if the 3rd Corps command sends an order to stop plunder, it would not send it to all brigades involved, in particular, since the 3rd Corps command was informed through the report of the OG Istok that the soldiers of several units were plundering in Vares. Now, the Defence also challenges the Trial Chamber's reliance on P468, which is a report prepared by the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Brigade informing Kubura that the collection of war booty had been carried out in an organised manner. The Defence points out that the report also states that looting was prevented. Now, the Trial Chamber was entitled to disregard this comment in P468 since there is a strong indication that there this is part of the report was self-serving. The report has been prepared by the very 7th Brigade who committed the plunder. I'd also like to draw your attention to a fourth piece of evidence that also supports that Mr. Kubura knew of the plunder in Vares, and that is Kubura's order of 7th November, 1993 to distribute the illegally appropriated property among members of 7th Brigade. That's trial judgement 1993. Kubura could not have given that order had he not known of the plunder. And finally, Mr. Kubura was the commander of the 7th Brigade and he was present in the area. The Trial Chamber found at paragraph 2091 that the organised scheme for the plunder in Vares could not have been implemented without prior approval of Kubura. Now, that concludes my submissions on Kubura's second ground of appeal, and we submit that Kubura's appeal should be dismissed in its entirety. Unless you have questions, that also concludes my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. There are no questions. So I would ask the Defence to make submissions in reply. In doing so, Mr. Dixon, may I ask you one question or clarification that may --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: -- allow me to better understand your position. You may take that into account in your submissions whenever you wish. You said in your previous submissions a couple of times that knowledge cannot be presumed and knowledge must be proved by direct evidence. I understand your point was that there is a need of specific evidence that proves knowledge on this specific date in which events occurred. Is that your point in terms of law, that knowledge cannot be proved but by direct evidence and would not be possible to prove knowledge by indirect evidence or circumstantial evidence? And if this is your position, why so? Can you explain me that. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I'll start with that question immediately. It is certainly not our position that knowledge can only be proved through the introduction of direct evidence. It can, of course, be proved from all of the circumstances taken together where the only reasonable conclusion is that the commander knew or had reason to know. Our submission is that there's both no direct evidence of Mr. Kubura knowing of any of these offences. He didn't witness them; there's no evidence of reports coming directly to him. But in addition to that, the circumstances don't allow the only reasonable inference to be drawn that he knew that his troops were directly involved in the commission of these crimes together with, as I've mentioned a few times, many other brigades and civilians as well. Your Honours, if I can move on to briefly reply. And the only issue which I'm going to address are the instances that my learned friend mentioned about other acts of plunder between June and November, in order to respond to the allegation that is put forward by the Prosecution that there's a repetitive pattern which -- which must have put Mr. Kubura on notice of events that were to follow in Vares in November 1993. I have, Your Honours, already addressed the point in relation to DH1553 and the related documents about these instances being really common crimes perhaps committed by members of the military but not in the context of -- of armed operations. Your Honours, in addition to that, there are certain references that were made by my learned friend in -- in relation to events that are in fact incorporated into the Vares count and the earlier Ovnak count. That would be in respect of the -- of the evidence of Witness ZA, talking about what happened in Ovnak a few days or a short period later, which is dealt with in -- in the count by -- by the Trial Chamber. And also, P674, which is Mr. Hadzihasanovic's order to Mr. Kubura in respect of Vares, and that deals directly, of course, with the events in Vares and it merely refers to the proper procedure in respect of war booty having to be followed. So in my submission, those kinds of references are of no use and of any relevance here. Secondly, the other category which -- which can be excluded, in my submission, would be those that refer to general orders about plundering. So -- so orders from the command which say that plundering should be prevented or forbidden in all circumstances, that the proper policies should be followed. Those are orders of a general nature and do not point to any specific incidents between June and November. The -- the only three that my -- my learned friend has referred Your Honours to are, one, an instance in respect of Cukle; another in the Fojnica sector; and then a reference to an order concerning looting in Kakanj. My submission initially, Your Honours, is, as you're aware, is that there were no particular incidents which Mr. Kubura could have been held responsible for under Article 7(3) or for which he was charged with in the indictment. Certainly, with regard to Cukle, as my learned friend has indicated, that was not charged against Mr. Kubura and no defence was -- was led obviously in respect of that allegation. And it's for that reason that the Trial Chamber at 1924 states that it considers that since the accused Kubura was not mentioned in the indictment in relation to the plunder committed in Cukle in June 1993, the question of measures taken by him need not be raised. So in our submission, that, too, is an incident that is of no relevance to this consideration, as it was not charged against Mr. Kubura and it was not a matter that therefore he had to address in respect of measures to be taken. Secondly, in respect of the Fojnica sector and the document referred to by the Prosecution is P814. I think it was referred to in the transcript as -- as P840, but it must be P814, dated 5 August 1993. And this is a report from the assistant commander for security of the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Brigade going to the assistant commander of security for the 7th Brigade command. So it's a report within the security sector of the brigade. And it -- it clearly indicates on -- on page 2 that a patrol was organised by the security sector to prevent any arson and looting. So the -- the nature of the report is -- is not indicating that looting occurred but indicating that steps were taken to prevent looting. So in our submission, it cannot be relied upon as evidence of looting occurring in that area, let alone Mr. Kubura knowing anything about, any allegations that were made in respect of looting. In our submission, there are none that appear on the face of this document. And it is also important, a point which I will return to when I respond to the Prosecution's appeal, to -- to note that with -- with many of these documents, including this one, there -- there was no evidence led before the Trial Chamber by the Prosecution of those persons who were involved in producing the documents or receiving the documents to -- to place them in their context, to allow for the parties to explore with the witnesses what were the circumstances in which this order was produced, and whether in fact it was a response to -- to any looting. What we are left with is merely what is on the face of the document, which is an indication that acts of looting should be prevented. And finally, Your Honours, the incident in respect of Kakanj, that is, P544. And that is a -- an order of 25 June coming from Mr. Hadzihasanovic to the deputy commander of the Supreme Command Staff. So it's an order going up, not -- not down, to any of the brigades of the 3rd Corps. And in this report, it is indicated that certain members of the 7th Brigade were relieved by the brigade command of their duties in Kakanj for failing to carry out an order to prevent crime and looting. So it is an indication, as far as we know, on -- on the face of -- of the document of steps being taken to prevent such action. Once again, not an instance that could be relied upon, in our submission, to find Mr. Kubura responsible as a commander under Article 7(3), and, in any event, a document which comes, again, without a context, without any other evidence, what exactly were these acts? We don't know. What steps were taken to prevent those acts taking place? We don't know. All we -- we are informed about is that steps were taken to relieve persons of their duties. Whether or not it is a matter that Mr. Kubura was involved in or had knowledge of, once again, is -- is a matter where there is no evidence on -- on the record. And it's for that reason that we maintain our position that there are no instances between June and November which Mr. Kubura could be held responsible for, which cumulatively could add up to him being on notice or upon which a conclusion can be drawn that he should have anticipated further actions occurring of an unlawful nature in November 1993. Your Honour, the final point that I wish to make is just in respect of the point that was made by my learned friend that there were no other brigades of the 3rd Corps involved in the operation in Vares, and he was referring to P448. There -- there are in that document a number of references to other brigades of the 3rd Corps: The 302, 304, to mention but a few. The brigades of the 3rd Corps naturally start with "3", and, for example, on page 12 there's a reference to -- to three brigades of the 3rd Corps being involved in the operation under the command of OG Istok participating in operations from the north and from the south, with a platoon of the 7th Brigade. And in our submission, this confirms what the Trial Chamber has found, that there were a number of units involved and a number of other groupings as well, including civilians, who were involved in looting in Vares. Your Honour, those are my submissions in reply, unless there are any further questions to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dixon. I see there are no further -- oh, well, Judge Guney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Dixon, I have a brief question, in the framework of the property seized in the Ovnak sector. Did the property seized in the Ovnak sector have any direct military use or the property in question was appropriated in an unlawful and deliberate manner and went beyond the scope of legitimate war booty? I would like to be enlightened on this question, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The appellant has not appealed against the Trial Chamber's finding that there was unlawful appropriation in -- in the Ovnak area in June 1993 of various forms of property and goods which would be outside of the policy of lawful war booty and would therefore be considered unlawful. The appellant has only appealed against whether Mr. Kubura knew that his particular subordinates were involved in -- in those actions, when there were a number of people whom the Trial Chamber found were responsible. The Trial Chamber wasn't able to specify which particular item on which particular moment was stolen or taken by which particular grouping or an individual civilian. It was a collective finding that various groupings were involved. And that particular finding has not been appealed. It's -- it's only what Mr. Kubura knew, whether he had reason to know or directly knew that his soldiers were involved in that action, and as a result of that, failed in his duty to -- to take certain steps. And, Your Honour, I can indicate that the same is applicable in respect of Vares as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, I think it's an appropriate time to break. We'll reconvene in 30 minutes, so that means 10.35. The hearing is suspended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So we'll resume the hearing. And according to the schedule, we move on to the Prosecution appeal. So we'll give the floor to the Prosecution for their submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Barbara Goy and I will be dealing with grounds 1 and 3 of the Prosecution appeal, the sentencing grounds. And Mr. Wirth will then address ground 2. And after that, Mr. Dalal will address ground 4. First addressing the ground of appeal. Enver Hadzihasanovic was found guilty --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: There is no transcript. Let's wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. I understand the transcript can be made later if we -- we may --if there is no disagreement, we may proceed. Is there any objection? No. If not, the Prosecution may --may start its submissions. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will start with the first ground of appeal. Enver Hadzihasanovic was found guilty under 7(3) for the murder of two people and the cruel treatment in Zenica music school, Orasac camp, and four different detention facilities in Bugojno. The Prosecution requests an increase of its sentence from five to ten years imprisonment. One of the murders was particularly heinous, the killing of Dragan Popovic. On 21 October 1993, Dragan Popovic was killed. His throat was cut and the head cut from his body. The soldier who finished the task proudly held up the disembodied head and forced other detainees to kiss it. Hadzihasanovic had the material ability to prevent this brutal ritualistic killing, but he failed to do so. Mladen Havranek, who was detained in the furniture salon in Bugojno, was called upstairs from the basement and the other detainees could hear him moaning and screaming and begging to stop the beating. After that, he could no longer walk, so the other prisoners dragged him back down to the basement. He lost consciousness and died as a result of the beating. Hadzihasanovic failed to adequately punish the perpetrators. Hadzihasanovic was also responsible as a superior for the terrible cruel treatment in the detention facilities, which lasted for several months. In Orasac camp, the cruel treatment was extremely violent. The prisoners were beaten with anything that came to hand, which led to broken bones, loss of consciousness. On top of the physical violence there, were death threats and harassments of every kind. At Zenica music school, the defenceless victims were constantly subjected to the cruellest physical abuse, often in front of other detainees. One detainee was kicked and punched until his face began to bleed copiously. Another had his hand tied up behind the back and was hit with a stick until his ribs were fractured. He could hardly walk or breathe. In other cases, the beatings resulted in a fractured skull, broken hands, even permanent damage, such as partial loss of eyesight and a need for hip replacement. These were just examples. The other detainees were beaten in the same way. The cruel treatment was repeated and the detainees lived in a permanent state of anxiety. The various detention facilities in Bugojno were also characterised by the particularly violent cruel treatment. In the furniture salon, the beating occurred virtually every night. Mladen Havranek died as a result of the mistreatment. Witness Alvir had broken ribs. When Witness ZH arrived at the Gimnazija school, he was beaten with rifle butts, kicked in the stomach, and once on the ground kicked in the kidney before he lost consciousness. After the beating he had a broken collarbone, lost 60 per cent of his right kidney function, and suffered two stomach hernias, which required surgery. The gravity of these crimes was ignored by the Trial Chamber. In addition, it took irrelevant mitigating factors into account. Gravity, as said by the Celebici appeals judgement, is a mandatory sentencing consideration for 7(3) liability as much as for 7(1). It requires to take into account the particular circumstances, including the nature of the crime --.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the Trial Chamber only paid lip service to this requirement by mentioning gravity in the section on legal framework for sentencing, but it did not apply these factors to the facts of this case. The part determination of sentence only refers to aggravating and mitigating factors. In sentencing, the Trial Chamber therefore only mentions the time span, the large number of victims of the cruel treatment, and the heinous character of the beheading under aggravating circumstances, not the impact on the victims who had to kiss the disembodied head. The sentence of the Trial Chamber thus fails to adequately capture the extent of Hadzihasanovic's culpability as a high-ranking military official who failed to prevent and punish very serious crimes. The Trial Chamber, moreover, erroneously mitigated the sentence by taking into account competence, effectiveness, intelligence, and good education and the lack of theoretical and practical training. Hadzihasanovic had been a professional soldier for 20 years. He was the former commander of a police battalion, so has particular experience with superior responsibility and its enforcement. Any lack of theoretical or practical training as a corps commander is irrelevant. I therefore invite you to grant the Prosecution's first ground of appeal. And unless there are questions regarding to the first ground of appeal, I would move to our third ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Liu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned about the gravity of the crime in the sentencing of Mr. Hadzihasanovic. I understand that the accused was convicted with the commander's responsibility. There's a question of law that when convicting somebody which the commander's responsibility, do we have to take into the gravity of the crime committed by his subordinate into the consideration, or we just take into account the seriousness of his omission of failing to prevent or punish his subordinate who committed the crime. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Our answer to that is that both factors have to be taken into account for Article 3 liability. The nature of the underlying crime, as set out in the Celebici appeal judgement in paragraph 732 is a factor to be taken into account as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: If there are no further questions regarding Hadzihasanovic, I would proceed with our appeal regarding Mr. Kubura's sentence. Two and a half years imprisonment for Amir Kubura is manifestly inadequate for two instances of plunder: The Trial Chamber ignored the gravity and should not have given any credit to Kubura for the finding that he obeyed an order to stop plunder in Vares. The Trial Chamber abused its discretion by taking into account in mitigation that Kubura swiftly complied with the order of the OG Istok on 4 November 1993 to stop the in Vares and to withdraw his troops. The fact that a commander follows the order to stop further commission of crimes is not mitigating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can you perhaps slow down --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: -- for the translation, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: In addition to giving credit to an irrelevant mitigating factor, the Trial Chamber ignored the gravity. Both in the Ovnak area and in Vares plunder was serious. In the avenue knock area -- Ovnak area, the lives of the victims were severely affected. Many houses were plundered. Right after the village fell, the 7th Brigade military police brought in trucks and took possession of technical equipment, household appliances, building materials, and food. The goods were assembled in a collection point in Brajkovici and then transported to the 7th Brigade headquarter in Bilmiste, which was set up as a collection point by Kubura. In Vares, the plunder was even worse. The soldiers plundered everything they could get their hands on. There was unrestrained plunder. They used force to achieve their aim. In order to commit looting, they destroyed shop windows and broke in doors. As described by one witness, every shop had at least a broken display window. Theft of foodstuff was part of the strategy of the troops plundering in Vares. And in both places, plunder was a systematic abuse of the war booty procedure. But Kubura did more than merely fail to prevent or punish. He accepted and organised the plunder. In Vares he effectively rewarded the plunderer by issuing a written order granting leave to the soldiers who took part in the operation and ordering the seized property to be distributed. However, only the systematic nature and the personal involvement were addressed in the sentencing part of the judgement as aggravating factors, which left the extent and level of violence used to achieve the plunder disregarded. The gravity of the plunder is not adequately reflected in the two and a half years imprisonment, particularly when taking into account that plunder as a war crime was punished by imprisonment of not less than five years in the SFRY Criminal Code. The Appeals Chamber should therefore consider what kind of message it is sending if a commander who not only fails to prevent and punish but in effect rewards his plundering troops need not fear a harsh punishment. This ends my submission on sentencing. And if there are no questions, Mr. Wirth will address you on ground 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: As Ms. Goy just indicated, I will be addressing you on the second ground of appeal. The Trial Chamber erred in acquitting Mr. Kubura for his failure to punish the destruction in Vares. It erred for at least two reasons: First, it failed to appreciate that Kubura knew that Vares had been plundered and that plundering a city usually goes hand-in-hand with destruction of shop fronts and doors simply to allow the perpetrators access to the goods that they wish to steal. This fact at least puts Kubura on inquiry notice. Second, the Trial Chamber failed to appreciate that the 3rd Corps command ordered the 7th Brigade to stop the destruction in Vares. Again, this at least provided inquiry notice to Kubura. On 4 November 1993, when the 7th Brigade entered the deserted town of Vares, chaos erupted. Not only did the soldiers steal everything they could steal; they also destroyed property on a large scale. As just has been pointed out to you, the soldiers of the 7th Brigade shattered shop fronts and broke down doors. This destruction was done for the sole purpose of plundering. That's trial judgement 1846. The result of the destruction was that practically all of the shops in Vares had shattered windows. Moreover, ABiH soldiers who appeared to be drunk went around shooting their weapons; thereby causing damage to buildings and houses. Trial judgement 1844. The soldiers of the 7th Brigade committed wholesale smashing of shop windows, making off with goods, and smashing cars. That's P448. This destruction reached such a level that the OG Istok expressed its alarm in two reports that were sent to the 3rd Corps command. That's P676 and P448. The 3rd Corps command reacted by issuing orders to the 7th Brigade. Excuse me, I seem to have misread the number of the second exhibit. It should be P446. The 3rd Command reacted by issuing orders to the 7th Brigade to stop the chaos and destruction and the looting. That's trial judgement 1986. Of course, the Trial Chamber had no doubt that the large-scale destruction committed by the 7th Brigade in Vares met the elements of the crime of destruction; however, the Trial Chamber found that Kubura was not responsible for this crime under Article 7(3) on the basis that it did not meet the mens rea requirements. This was an error. At the very least, Kubura was on inquiry notice. The Trial Chamber committed either an error of law or an error of fact, and we addressed that in our appeal brief. Today I will limit myself to the factual argument. No reasonable Trial Chamber could have concluded that Kubura had no inquiry notice for the destruction in Vares. Now, in order to establish that Kubura knew of the destruction, the Trial Chamber had to find that he had at least reason to know that his subordinates committed destruction in Vares. The Blaskic appeals judgement in paragraph 64 states that: "The authoritative interpretation for the term 'reason to know' is still to be found in the Celebici appeals judgement." According to Celebici, the information that is received by the commander must not compel the conclusion that a crime was committed. It is sufficient if it indicates the need for further inquiry. Celebici appeals judgement, paragraphs 236 and paragraph 241. In this case, there are two evidentiary bases which both independently show that Kubura had sufficiently alarming information that the 7th Brigade had committed destruction. The first basis was that Kubura knew that the 7th Brigade had looted the whole town. This in and of itself automatically raises the question as to how did the perpetrators gain access to the looted goods if not through the destruction of shop fronts and doors; in other words, destruction goes hand-in-hand with the looting of a city. And this was exactly the case in Vares. The Trial Chamber found that the destruction of shop fronts and doors in Vares was committed with the sole purpose of committing plunder. Given all this information, the fact that Kubura knew that the town of Vares had been looted, as a minimum indicated to him that it was necessary to further investigate whether the soldiers that had committed the plunder -- his soldiers that had committed the plunder also had committed the necessary correlate of such plunder, and that is the crime of destruction. Now, the second basis for Kubura's inquiry notice is the order of the 4th of November to prevent chaos, looting, and destruction in Vares. This order was received by the 7th Brigade. That's trial judgement 1852. And it was used by the Trial Chamber to establish that Kubura knew of the crime of plunder in Vares. Paragraph 1986. The order is referred to in P446, the report of the 3rd Corps command to the OG Istok. The report explicitly states that the order was that destruction in Vares had to be prevented. Again, at a minimum, Kubura was put on notice by this order that he needed to investigate whether the 7th Brigade, his troops who were on the ground, who were in Vares, was involved in such destruction. A simple inquiry. A simple inquiry with his soldiers, the 3rd Corps command, the OG Istok, all international organisations who were present on the ground, would have revealed the 7th Brigade was responsible for the destruction. In summary, no reasonable Trial Chamber could have found that Kubura did not possess the necessary mens rea for failure to punish destruction in Vares. And the Prosecution therefore requests that the Appeal Chamber convict Kubura under count 5 for failure to punish the crime of wanton destruction in Vares and to increase the sentence accordingly. That would conclude my submissions, unless Your Honours have questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Liu has a question. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, are you suggesting to us that the Trial Chamber bases the finding regarding Kubura's knowledge of the plunder as well as destruction on the same set of the documents? Namely, you know, the orders, the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We are -- we are saying that the order that is mentioned in P446 provided sufficient inquiry notice that destruction had been committed by the 7th Brigade. Obviously we also have -- I just set out a second basis for that inquiry notice, and that is the sheer fact that plunder -- that he was aware that plunder had been committed, as was found by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: There are no other questions. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Thank you. Then Mr. Marwan Dalal will now address you on our fourth ground. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Marwan Dalal, and I will be presenting the fourth ground of the Prosecution's appeal, which relates to significant -- to an error in the trial judgement that is significant to the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. This ground does not have, of course, an impact on the verdict of the Trial Chamber. The content of this ground is the duty of a superior under Article 7(3) of the Statute to punish subordinates or a subordinate for the commission of a serious violation of the laws and customs of war of a war crime. Also, the Prosecution submits that disciplinary measures as such are not sufficient for the commander, for the superior to discharge his duty under Article 7(3) of the Statute to punish subordinates. And here I would like to clarify for the Chamber that the Prosecution submissions relate to disciplinary measures. And if the term "summary disciplinary measure" had caused any confusion, the Prosecution takes full responsibility for this, but the Prosecution would like to make it clear that we address the disciplinary measures as such being not sufficient for discharging the duty of a commander under Article 7(3) to punish subordinates for the commission of war crimes. The Prosecution's position is that the duty of a superior under Article 7(3) must include the -- the duty to punish must include reporting the matter to the competent prosecutorial judicial authority. The situation before us is very clear; we have a superior who either knows or had reason to know about the commission of serious violations of customary international humanitarian law and he is faced with a choice how to discharge his duty to punish. The Prosecution submits that in order for this choice to be legal, it must include reporting the matter for -- or reporting the matter to the competent prosecutorial judicial authorities. The superior cannot -- the military commander cannot confine the matter of punishment to internal disciplinary measures of the military itself. This is not to ask the impossible from the superior. On the contrary, it is to obligate him to do the reasonable, the necessary, and the right thing at the same time. I will now move on to identify the legal error of the Trial Chamber, and then argue the four points that in the Prosecution's submission, constitute the duty of the superior to punish by -- by reporting the matter to the judicial -- to the competent prosecutorial judicial authorities.
