The Trial Chamber erred when it found that 30 to 60 days imprisonment as a disciplinary measure taken by a superior was sufficient to discharge the duty to punish for plunder. And in case I had not clarified, this submission relates to the war crime of plunder. This -- this finding of the Trial Chamber contradicts Article 142 of the SFRY Criminal Code, which imposed a minimum of five years imprisonment for the crime of plunder as a war crime. It also does not correlate with the Trial Chamber on finding in paragraph 2041 that the plunder was widespread and significant. In paragraph 1777, the Trial Chamber had correctly described the law in relation to other crimes under Article 3 of the Statute; namely, murder and mistreatment, which the Prosecution in -- in the Prosecution's submission, it is the correct law. The error, of course, not applying this law on the crime of plunder. I will quote briefly what the Trial Chamber said about the duty of a superior to report the matter to the competent judicial authorities. "The Chamber cannot over-emphasize that in international law a superior has a duty to take the necessary and reasonable measures to punish those who violate the laws or customs of war. The accused Hadzihasanovic could not consider as acceptable punishment the disciplinary sanction of a period of detention not exceeding 60 days. He had the duty to take specific measures to ensure that the perpetrators were prosecuted and to report accordingly." Your Honours are also referred to the Strugar trial judgement in paragraph 376, the Kordic trial judgement in paragraph 446, and the Halilovic trial judgement, paragraph 97/98, that support this description of the law. The four points that in the Prosecution's submission establish the duty of the superior to report to the competent prosecutorial authorities the commission of a war crime by his subordinate as a measure of punishment are the gravity of the crime of plunder, the insufficiency of disciplinary measures, the duty imposed by customary international humanitarian law on superiors to report such crimes to the competent prosecutorial authorities, and lastly, the state's duty to investigate and prosecute war crimes mandates also the superior to report the issue to the competent prosecutorial judicial authorities. Your Honours, the gravity of plunder cannot be over-emphasized nor contested. Plunder as a war crime had been -- has been defined as such, at least for the last 100 years. It is prescribed in Article 3 of the ICTY Statute; Article 4 of the ICTR Statute; Article 8 of the International Criminal Court Statute; and Article 4 of the Second Protocol additional to the Geneva Conventions; Article 33 of the 4th Geneva Convention; the Charter of the International Military Tribunal in Nuremberg; Article 6, and also in Articles 28 and 47 of The Hague Regulations concerning the laws or customs of war. Plunder has accompanied the laws and customs of war as a serious crime if committed, as I mentioned, for a long time, and one cannot underestimate or over-emphasize the gravity of this grave. The gravity as such imposes a duty on the superior to transfer or to refer, to report the matter to the competent prosecutorial authorities when he knows or had reason to know that his subordinates committed such a crime. In addition, disciplinary measures alone can never be sufficient to discharge a superior's duty to punish under Article 7(3) of the Statute. Military discipline, as they are, are their purpose and they are designed to look inwards into the military, to regulate the relationship between superior and subordinate, and the functioning, the proper functioning of the military. Its purpose is not to punish war crimes. They could be part of the measures taken to punish war crimes, but they could never be alone, by themselves, sufficient to discharge a duty to punish war crimes by a superior. In paragraph 948 of the trial judgement, there's a description of the conduct that triggers -- that triggered the application of disciplinary measures. The Trial Chamber mentions, for example, the conduct of desertion, abandoning one's post, refusing to fight or disobeying soldiers. These are, Your Honours, not war crimes and cannot be considered as war crimes. These are internal matters for the military that do not take into account the outside of the military, as war crimes or the punishment of war crimes should be taken. Your Honours are also referred to the Rules of military discipline of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, P325 and Articles 3 and 7 in that exhibit, where there's a description what is the conduct that is punishable through disciplinary measures, and, of course, none of them mentions war crimes. Disciplinary measures are often initiated unilaterally by the military commander based on his discretion. Most importantly, it imposes -- these measures impose minimal sanctions compared with the serious violations of laws and customs of war. I refer Your Honours to Exhibit P120, decree law on service in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which stipulates the sanctions that could be imposed through disciplinary measures. These include, for example, admonition, reprimand, overtime duty of up to three shifts, confinement to leave the barracks compound for up to four days, demotion to a lower rank, prison for up to 60 days. These and other disciplinary measures are not reasonable by themselves to punish a war crime, including the war crime of plunder. The insufficiency of this measure also imposes a duty on the superior to report the matter to the competent prosecutorial and judicial authorities. Customary international humanitarian law imposes a duty, a clear duty, on the superior to report the war crime to the competent prosecutorial authorities. By reporting we mean - and without exhausting the list - noting the place of the crime, the plunder; who were the subordinate units or individuals who had -- who had participated in plunder, or subordinates or individuals who had been at the scene of the crime; and also reporting the reports that the superior should be asking from his subordinates about what happened at the scene of the crime, sending these reports to the competent prosecutorial authorities. Article 87(1) as well as Article 87(3) of the First Additional Protocol of the Geneva Convention of 1977 impose such a duty. ICRC commentary on Article 87 interprets this duty by saying that it includes, and I'm quoting, "Remitting the case to the judicial authority, where necessary, with such factual evidence as it was possible to find." I refer Your Honours to ICRC commentary, paragraph 3562, page 1023. In addition, the Statute of the International Criminal Court at Article 28 explicitly stipulates this duty by saying that "The superior will incur criminal liability if he failed" - and I'm quoting - "to submit the matter to the competent authorities for investigation and prosecution." These clear duties, under customary international humanitarian law, are supplemented by state practice which include laws in national jurisdictions that also define such a duty of a superior to report the matter to the competent prosecutorial judicial authorities when knowing or having a reason to know about the commission of a war crime. And I refer Your Honours to such legislation in Canada, Germany, Australia, and England, and I refer Your Honours to paragraph 5.25 of the Prosecution appeal brief, where these laws are referred to explicitly. Finally, Your Honours, the duty of states to investigate and prosecute war crimes are another source for imposing a duty on the superior to report the matter in question to the competent prosecutorial authorities because without such a duty on the superior, the duty of states could be rendered meaningless. There's a clear link between the knowledge of the superior and his material ability to take measures and of the state to implement its duty to investigate and prosecute war crimes. The duty of states to investigate and prosecute war crimes are enshrined in Article 86 of the First Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions and also in Rule 158 of the ICRC Study on Customary International Humanitarian Law, which stipulates: "States must investigate war crimes allegedly committed by their nationals or armed forces or on their territory and, if appropriate, prosecute the suspects." This is in volume 1 of the study, page 607. In conclusion, Your Honours, reporting the matter, reporting the commission of a war crime of plunder to the competent prosecutorial judicial authorities is a reasonable measure and a necessary one. The superior can and should report about the commission of the war crime, the location of its perpetration, the identity of individuals or units who perpetrated the war crime or who were at the scene of the crime, as well as to transfer reports from his subordinates about the commission of the war crime. Reporting to the competent prosecutorial judicial authority must be therefore a clear duty imposed on the superior in order for him not to incur criminal liability under Article 7(3) for failing to punish. Based on all of our submissions, Your Honours, the -- unless Your Honours have questions, of course, the Prosecution respectfully requests the granting of the relief sought in the appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, President. Counsel, is your complaint or argument institutional; namely, disciplinary versus criminal proceedings? Or is it related to the maximum penalties that can be imposed? Imagine for a moment that you have disciplinary proceedings that allow the imposition, say, of five years imprisonment. Would you have a quarrel with that too?

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: It is -- our quarrel is -- relates to both. It relates to the procedure as such and the minimal sanction that we identified in many states as -- in the supplement of our brief that usually the sanction is minimal and the procedure is quick. The procedure, as I have indicated, relates to the direct relationship commander-subordinate, and organising and regulating the relationships within the military itself. So based on the experience of many national jurisdictions that we identified in the appendix to our brief, we can say that usually the sanction is minimal. But if there's a theoretical example or actual, concrete exception that the sanction is high, this could give a consideration to the matter. However, the procedure issue is very important and war crime deserves both a sincere -- a serious procedure as a means of punishment and an adequate sanction. So it is a cumulative matter, not to select procedure over sanction or the opposite, or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Counsel, my mind is open on this subject and I'm grateful to you for your arguments. Tell me, when one speaks of the duty of a superior to prevent or punish, does punishment there have the same meaning as punishment by a court of law?

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: The duty of the superior of a military commander is to take the reasonable and necessary measures. Usually, of course, he doesn't have the authority to prosecute. So we cannot say that he has a duty the same as the competent prosecutorial or judicial authorities. But as -- but the Prosecution submits that he is an important link leading to an adequate procedure and sanction of a war crime, and this link of reporting is indeed part of his duty as a superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Meron quite rightly pointed out to you some disciplinary sanctions could be severe. Now, do you say that a superior officer who has imposed a disciplinary sanction of severity has not punished the subordinate in question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: He has punished. And we can always find probably these exceptional situations of having the disciplinary measure including a severe sanction. However, on the empiric almost study, I should say, that the Prosecution has on the matter, detailed in the appendix to our submissions, written submissions, we could not find a place almost that the disciplinary measure included such severe sanction. Again, I repeat the submission that it is the punishment of a war crime deserves these two elements: A serious procedure, not a quick, hasty one; and a -- and an adequate sanction, which fits the gravity of the war crime as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, I shall, of course, read back your written case and, in particular, the appendix to which you referred, but do you offhand have any written authority you would care to refer me to on the subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: On the subject of the duty of the superior?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. On the subject which you are raising, that a disciplinary sanction is not a sufficient measure to discharge the duty of a superior officer to punish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: If Your Honour means by "authority" an academic article by a leading academic, we don't have as such. But the Prosecution's position is that the clear understanding and interpretation of the duty of a commander under Article 87 of the First Protocol of the Geneva Conventions and its interpretation by -- or the commentary by the ICRC clearly lead to the conclusion that there is such a duty, combined with the explicit mentioning of the matter in the Statute of the International Criminal Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Counsel, you may well be right. I shall have to look it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I understand this concludes your response. There are no other questions. If -- sorry, your appeal. I was saying "your response." Now, so we can move to the responses. Okay. So we start -- according to the schedule, the response by Hadzihasanovic Defence. So please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May it please the Court. [In English] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning Honourable Judges of the Appeals Chamber. Before I begin, allow me to say that this is both for my colleague and I a -- an honour and a privilege to appear before you this morning. This is a first for both my colleague and I, having both been working at the International Tribunal for some ten years, and it does have a special meaning for us. Personally, when I was invited more than six years ago now as proceedings were beginning against General Hadzihasanovic in July of 2001, I was invited to join his Defence team and I decided to leave the comfort of a secure United Nations position working for the Honourable Judges of the Court in order to undertake this important endeavour. Little did I know then that more than six years later I would be standing before you in this very -- very same Appeals Chamber and in the same case, handling the proceedings against General Hadzihasanovic. I insist on the figure "more than six years" because it is, in our submission, included in the impact of these proceedings, the impact that these proceedings have had on General Hadzihasanovic ever since he was charged in July of 2001 and immediately surrendered in the custody of the International Tribunal. We believed then, Mr. President, that the command responsibility charges laid against General Hadzihasanovic were not warranted, and as can be seen from the grounds of appeal raised against the trial judgement, which we will address tomorrow, we still believe that this is the case. Nonetheless, we must today respond to the Prosecution's submission that the sentence of five years imposed on General Hadzihasanovic was manifestly inadequate and unreasonable. In this regard, Mr. President, we submit - and I will have the opportunity to do so tomorrow - that the Trial Chamber committed numerous errors during the trial of General Hadzihasanovic, errors of law, errors of fact, as well as errors which have impeded on the appellant's right to a fair trial. In our submission, however, sentencing is not one of those errors. That is, of course, on the basis of the counts for which General Hadzihasanovic was found guilty, and that is eight specific incidents based on two counts; whereas, he was tried for 29 different incidents based on seven counts. Looking specifically at the eight incidents for which the Trial Chamber found General Hadzihasanovic guilty, we are of the view that the sentence could have been lower. We came to this conclusion on the basis of both his role and the form and degree of his participation, as well as the gravity of the incidents for which he was found guilty and those for which he was found not guilty. That being said, we could not identify any discernible error on regard of the -- in this regard on the part of the Trial Chamber. There is, in our submission, no error which could warrant a reduction and no error which could justify or require an increase in sentence. Consequently, our position on the Prosecution's appeal is, as expressed in our written pleadings, the following: Firstly, we believe that the adjudication of our appeal, that is, the appeal lodged on behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, will render the Prosecution's appeal ground on sentencing moot. Secondly, should that not be the case, there are no reasons or justifications to modify the sentence imposed. The first issue I would like to address in response to the Prosecution appeal on sentence is the character of the respondent who stands before you today and whom you will have the opportunity of hearing tomorrow. The Prosecution did not address the character of General Hadzihasanovic in its argument. It is our respectful submission that the main issues in this Prosecution appeal over above -- and I weigh my words -- over and above the gravity of the crimes for which he was found guilty, which was considered by the Trial Chamber, we believe that the main issues are the character of the accused, the manner in which he exercised his command in the most difficult of circumstances, and the form and degree of participation of General Hadzihasanovic in the crimes for which he was found guilty. Without repeating our submissions in our written pleadings, we do feel that it is important to draw the attention of the Appeals Chamber on some of these issues. We need to remind and we wish to recall the Appeals Chamber that this is a case of a commander who, despite impossible circumstances, succeeded in accomplishing the mission he was entrusted with, which is the overall objective of a commander, while at the same time taking countless measures to prevent his subordinates from committing violations of international humanitarian law and breaches of discipline alike and to have them punished if they did. General Hadzihasanovic, throughout his tenure as commander of the 3rd Corps, a period of approximately ten months, stressed the importance of training for his troops, including training on international humanitarian law. In relation to the military police, the Trial Chamber found that General Hadzihasanovic had reminded on several occasions the military police or the Military Police Battalion to take all necessary measures to detect and prevent criminal activities. The policy of the 3rd Corps in this respect is clear and stands out from the evidence. Following orders of General Hadzihasanovic, the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion filed no less than 377 criminal reports involving 804 identified and 20 unidentified persons; that is, during the period from 14 September 1992 to 1 March of 1994. This, Mr. President, the Trial Chamber did refer in its judgement. However, there's further evidence which the Trial Chamber did not refer to in its judgement which we feel is relevant at this point in time. The Trial Chamber did not refer to document DH119. This is a report from the Travnik District Military Prosecutor for the year 1993. According to this report, no less than 823 criminal reports were filed before the district military prosecutor against 1.044 persons. From these persons, 8 -- sorry, 627 were ordinary members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 386 were conscripts, also members of the army. The Trial Chamber did not refer also to another important exhibit, DH274. This is a report from the Zenica District Military Court, a different district. The report deals with the -- with the report -- with the period from 1 January until 10 December of 1993. During this period, different district, different court, 432 criminal cases were laid against persons of members of the 3rd Corps of the Army of Yugoslavia -- Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina against 869 individuals. The types of offences which were looked at by all of these reports are mentioned in the one report which the Trial Chamber did refer to, and that was DH155.2, and the types of offences include 16 identified perpetrators in relation to murders; 8 for involuntary manslaughter; 9 for grievous bodily harm; 1 for double murder; and 1 for violent conduct. Violent conduct in this regard refers to Article 204 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY, which I will refer to tomorrow in one of my arguments. Mr. President, when I look at -- sorry. When I look at the Prosecution appeal, first we must look in the manner in which he exercised his command, but also we also must refer to the arguments of the Prosecution concerning the gravity of the crimes, which it says was ignored. We believe, Mr. President, that the gravity of -- factor was not ignored by the Trial Chamber. The gravity factor includes both the crimes themselves - we agree with the Prosecution on this - and the form and degree of participation of the accused. It is our submission that the Trial Chamber considered both and that it stands out from our written submissions. We also submit, Mr. President, that the Trial Chamber rightly focused on the form and -- and degree of participation based on the fact that this is exclusively a command responsibility case. The Trial Chamber did conclude that nothing in the evidence would allow the responsibility of the respondent to be assimilated or linked to individual responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute. In this regard, it is indeed very important to focus on the seriousness of the omission, to use the words of one of your -- of the Honourable members of this Appeals Chamber. The Prosecution's argument regarding rank and position, we respectfully submit, are misconceived. It is simply not automatic that when you have a high-ranking superior, he deserves a harsher punishment. There are instances where this will be the case, as explained in our written pleadings, and there are instances where it will be the contrary, and this will work to his advantage. Looking at the seriousness of the omission, it is important to note the distance between the accused, now the respondent, and the events which took place or the crime which were committed; for example, the beheading in Orasac. The beheading in Orasac, it is, of course, a very severe event, a very grave crime, something that we would all like to avoid, but we have to also remember it took place at a place when no one within the 3rd Corps was even aware that civilians had been taken to a camp in Orasac. When we assess the severity of the omission, these events -- these factors must be taken into consideration. Regarding the Prosecution's argument misapplication of good character, we submit that the Trial Chamber did not make any mistake, did not make any mistake in considering the intelligence and good education of General Hadzihasanovic, as well as his lack of theoretical and practical training. One issue not mentioned today by the Prosecution but which is found in its brief refers to the fact that the sentence -- or the crimes of which he was found guilty would have attracted a minimum penalty of five years in the former Republic of Yugoslavia. We believe that this argument is incorrect, as has been explained in our brief. And I refer more specifically to Articles 41, 42, and 43 of the Criminal Code of the Socialist Republic of the former Yugoslavia, which explains why this is not the case. And I'll be glad to answer any questions you may have in this regard. It follows, Mr. President, that the Trial Chamber did not commit any discernible error regarding sentencing and there is no reason for the Appeals Chamber to disturb the finding or the sentence imposed by the Trial Chamber. If I have a few minutes, I can address quickly the last ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Two minutes, but Judge Meron wants to address a point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Just very briefly, a question of clarification. You mentioned cases referred to the military prosecutor. They appear not to involve destruction or plunder of property? Is my understanding correct? And if it is, why?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Judge, thank you very much for your question. This report, I simply highlighted the gravest crime against person, but they also included all other types of crimes. But my aim was to highlight that General Hadzihasanovic did not let anything go unpunished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And the other crimes - namely, property crimes - also let to prosecutions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. In some cases, yes; in some cases, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: With regard to the last ground of appeal, I will make a very quick argument. Simply to say that we disagree with the Prosecution's submission because it doesn't focus on the responsibilities and the duties of the commander. What is important when dealing with Article 7(3) of the Statute is to deal with whether the measures taken or the failure to take measures is a necessary and reasonable character of the measures. In some cases, a disciplinary punishment might be sufficient. In other cases, a criminal report will indeed be required. In some cases, an investigation or reporting the matter to a superior officer will be sufficient. Thank you very much, Mr. President. This concludes my argument. I will be glad to answer any questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: There are no questions. Well, we're a bit ahead of schedule, but perhaps it's wise to break now, because -- unless -- unless Kubura's Defence would start for ten minutes, but then we have to break. So it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps it would be best to have the break now and then do it in one go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That's fine. So we'll have the break now for 20 minutes. That means at 12.10 we'll reconvene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So the hearing is resumed. I will now give the floor to the Defence of Mr. Kubura for their response.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You have the floor, Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will not be --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We apologise, Your Honour, for being late.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will not be addressing the fourth ground of the Prosecution's appeal, as it has no impact on Mr. Kubura's appeal or our response to the Prosecution's appeal. I will limit my submissions to grounds 2 and 3, starting with the destruction in Vares. Our response is in two parts: Firstly, there's no error of law that the Prosecution has shown. The Trial Chamber quite clearly stated - and this is at paragraph 1853 - that it did not find that the Prosecution had proved that the respondent knew or had reason to know of destruction. It did not limit its finding to -- to actual knowledge. It looked at the component of reason to know as well. And certainly, in taking into consideration the various orders and reports that the Prosecution have referred to, it is evident that they were looking not only at actual knowledge and direct knowledge but also all of the surrounding circumstances to determine whether any inference could be drawn from that evidence which could suggest that there were reasons to know of the destruction. Secondly, the -- the other error of law referred to by -- by the Prosecution also has no merit, in our submission. The Trial Chamber did not find that there was a requirement of a superior's certainty of the commission of crimes. It applied the well-established standard of proof that the Trial Chamber must be certain or sure that the evidence shows that the accused knew or had reason to know of the crimes. This is the well-established standard of beyond reasonable doubt. And that is at paragraph 1852. Your Honour, in addition, in our submission, the findings of the Trial Chamber need to be looked at in the context of the judgement as a whole. And I refer Your Honours here to paragraphs 309 and 311 of -- of the judgement, where at paragraph 311 the Trial Chamber specifically notes that it subscribes to the idea that although an inference can be made from direct or circumstantial evidence, it must be reasonable and narrowly construed. Consequently, the Chamber rejects any inferences based on a series of inferences. In addition, in cases where several inferences may be made on the basis of the same evidence and they are equally plausible, the Chamber considered that it could not hold the most prejudicial evidence against the accused, except in cases where the inference most favourable to the accused cannot be upheld in view of the facts of the case. In our submission, a perfectly reasonable mode of analysing the evidence and applying the correct standard of proof, which we say was done in respect of the -- the charge of destruction in Vares. Moving on then to the second part of -- of this appeal ground. There was no error of fact, in our submission, either. The Trial Chamber has considered all the evidence. The Prosecution has not asserted that the Trial Chamber overlooked any piece of evidence, and it has not found beyond reasonable doubt that that evidence showed the requisite knowledge. In particular, the Trial Chamber found that the orders of the operational group command to the 3rd Corps on 4 November - and we've referred to these a number of times now, but for the record, those two orders are P445 and P676 - and the 3rd Corps command response on the same day, that being order P446, the Trial Chamber found that they do not on their face establish Mr. Kubura's knowledge of destruction. It is worth taking into account at this point that there was no other evidence before the Trial Chamber concerning these particular documents. No witnesses were called to explain the context of these documents, how they were to be interpreted or implemented. And the Trial Chamber at para 297 and the paragraphs that follow provides an explanation, an analysis of how it viewed such documents. I will only read paragraph 297, where the Trial Chamber says: "The Chamber obviously attached more weight to documents witnesses explained in a convincing fashion than to documents submitted in isolation, and therefore without a witness's comments and observations." Once again, a perfectly reasonable conclusion, in -- in our submission. There was, thus, no evidence that the 3rd Corps command in the context of those orders expressed any concern to Mr. Kubura after it had received reports of destruction from the OG command. The Trial Chamber explicitly says at paragraph 1852 that it is possible that some concerns were expressed but it finds that the evidence does not show that that is established beyond reasonable doubt. In other words, to apply the jurisprudence that the Prosecution referred to, the Trial Chamber found that it was not proved beyond reasonable doubt that there was information conveyed to Mr. Kubura which indicated that there was destruction or that further inquiry was needed. In our submission, a reasonable Trial Chamber could have reached such a conclusion on the evidence. And the reasoning of the Trial Chamber cannot be faulted in this regard. Moreover, Your Honours, in our submission, the Prosecution is wrong to suggest that because a commander has knowledge of acts of plunder, it follows that he must also have knowledge of other crimes. It is, in our submission, the most basic of principles that the Prosecution must prove the requisite knowledge for the particular crimes charged, whether those be plunder or destruction or cruel treatment, and so forth. The Prosecution is, in our submission, wrong to assert that the evidence in respect of plunder in Vares was the same as the -- the evidence that the Prosecution relied upon in respect of destruction. This is set out in more detail in our response brief at paragraphs 13 through to 15. In particular, I would draw Your Honours' attention to P468, an order from the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Brigade, which I referred to in my earlier submission, which was a particular document relied upon by the Trial Chamber in respect of plunder, which did not apply to destruction and for which there are no similar documents in respect of destruction. Also, document P675, which was the -- the document, Your Honours will recall, that required the commander of the 7th Brigade to take action, did only mention that action was required to prevent goods from being removed. There's no mention of destruction, a distinction, in our submission, that a reasonable Trial Chamber could certainly make and place reliance upon in determining whether all of the evidence showed beyond reasonable doubt that Mr. Kubura knew or had reason to know. And finally, Your Honours, there was no finding of destruction in respect of Ovnak in June 1993. Mr. Kubura was acquitted of failing to prevent or punish destruction in the Ovnak area. That was in respect of count 5. And this is a -- a verdict which the Prosecution has not appealed, so there can be no suggestion of a continuing pattern starting in Ovnak and continuing through to Vares. Lastly on -- on this point of an error of fact, the -- the Prosecution has drawn Your Honours' attention to the document which I've just mentioned, P675, as a document which orders that all unauthorised acts are to cease. In our submission, this document cannot be interpreted to refer to destruction on its face. The unauthorised acts are not specified, and nor are any units specified, as I reiterated earlier, in this multi-brigade operation. And it is significant that there is no specific mention of destruction. Once again, the Trial Chamber acted perfectly reasonably, in our submission, in finding that that document, amongst a series of documents, did not cross [Realtime transcript read in error "Kosovo"] the threshold of proving knowledge beyond a reasonable doubt. In sum, Your Honours there, has been no error in the reasoning of the Trial Chamber which has resulted in a miscarriage of justice, and the Appeals Chamber is thus respectfully invited to reject this ground of appeal from the Prosecution. I will now move on now to the final ground, ground 3, in respect of sentence. Your Honour, there's one correction to the transcript, and that's at page 36, line 3. I didn't mention the word "Kosovo." I mentioned the word "cross" the threshold of proving knowledge. A small correction. In -- in respect of sentence, Your Honour, our submission is that the Trial Chamber probably -- properly took into account all relevant factors, and there are -- are five points only which I wish to make, briefly, in this regard, all relevant factors which were taken into account and properly assessed by the -- the Trial Chamber. Firstly, that -- this case in respect of Mr. Kubura is a somewhat unusual one in that the sole conviction is for failing to prevent and/or punish looting under Article 7(3), when he was acquitted of all of the more serious offences. Secondly, as was indicated in the president's order of 11 April 2006, property-related crimes are to be regarded in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, and indeed national jurisdictions, as relatively less serious crimes than those against the person. And that's at paragraph 8 of the 11 April 2006 order. Thirdly, it is significant, in our submission, that the Prosecution initially recommended ten years of imprisonment for Mr. Kubura for the entire indictment, which included over 30 murders, detentions, and cruel treatment. In our submission, it would be wholly disproportionate for the Prosecution now to suggest that a sentence for failing to punish two instances of looting on two days should be any higher than that imposed by the Trial Chamber, especially considering that we are only talking about convictions for two counts out of sixteen and for property-related offences only. The recommendation of the Prosecution is found at transcript reference 19108 to 19109. Fourthly, it is, of course, well-established in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal that sentences should not be out of reasonable proportion with a line of sentencing passed in similar circumstances for -- for the same offences. There are no similar cases, in respect of this particular one, and I add as well that persons have not been charged before the Bosnian war crimes national courts to date purely for property-related crimes. However, what can be said with -- with some certainty is that this sentence is on the lower end of the scale and should remain so, in comparison to slightly higher and higher sentences that have been passed and approved for more serious crimes against person. And lastly, Your Honours, in our submission, it must be mitigation if steps are taken to prevent the continuation of a crime. If the evidence is that as soon as a person knows or is on notice that a crime may be being committed and steps are taken to intervene, that is a factor which must be taken into consideration and most properly taken into consideration by the Trial Chamber as a mitigating factor, as opposed to allowing, which could be regarded as aggravating, crimes to continue indefinitely. So in our submission, there are no manifest errors in the reasoning of the Trial Chamber in respect of sentence and the Prosecution's appeal in that respect should be rejected as well. Those are my submissions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dixon. Any questions from the Bench? I don't think it's the case. We can move on to hear the reply by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll be very short on the reply with regard to the first and second ground of appeal. Counsel for Mr. Kubura stated that there was no evidence that the 3rd Corps command expressed concern with regard to the destruction in Vares. Now, that is not entirely correct. As we know from Exhibit P446, the 3rd Corps command sent an order to stop the destruction, inter alia the destruction. The only thing that is not expressly spelled out in P446 with regard to the contents on the -- of the order is who were the perpetrators. The 7th Brigade is not mentioned in P446. And in that regard, our submission is that Kubura had at least inquiry notice. He at least needed to go and look whether his own troops were involved in that plunder about which the 3rd Corps command did express concern. The second point I'd like to make is Defence counsel's submission that it is wrong that acts of plunder imply knowledge of acts of destruction. Well, that's not exactly our submission. Our submission is that if a perpetrator knows that a whole city has been looted -- excuse me, if an accused knows that a whole city has been looted, that that puts him on inquiry notice to find out how the perpetrators could have achieved the looting. And in this case, as in many other cases where towns are looted, it has been achieved by breaking shop fronts and -- and breaking in doors. The third point is that counsel mentioned there was no finding of destruction in Ovnak. Now, that is correct, but the reason why there was no finding is because the Trial Chamber was not able to distinguish between the destruction carried out by the Croat forces and the destruction carried out by ABiH troops. That's in -- and the Trial Chamber was therefore unable to identify the perpetrators of the destruction that had happened in Ovnak. That's paragraph 1832. Now, in Vares we do know that the perpetrators of the destruction were members of the 7th Brigade, and that is the distinction. That would end my reply, unless Your Honours have questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't believe there is any further question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Then my colleague Ms. Barbara Goy will now reply to the sentencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: I will first briefly reply to the issues raised by the Defence for Hadzihasanovic. The Defence has pointed to the context of the good character and the manner of command of Hadzihasanovic. The Trial Chamber took both of these factors into account in paragraph 2080. It took into account that he had a character that can be rehabilitated and inter alia relied on the prior -- lack of prior criminal record and prior good reputation, which the Prosecution has not challenged, and also relied on the fact that he worked to enforce the rules of IHL. Regarding the gravity for liability under 7(3), as well as the points raised on the Yugoslav law, we rely on our brief. And for the last part, particularly refer Your Honours to paragraphs 2.22 through 2.24 of our reply brief. With regard to the sentencing appeal regarding Kubura, the Defence seems to suggest that it is incompatible for the Prosecution to have at trial requested a sentence of ten years imprisonment and despite all the acquittals, now appealing the sentence of two and a half years as manifestly inadequate. This seems to imply that the sentence is composed of an addition of individual sentences for the underlying convictions. However, according to Rule 87(C), the Trial Chamber can either impose a sentence in respect of each finding of guilt and say whether it's to be served consecutively or concurrently, or like in this case, impose a single sentence which reflects the totality of the criminal conduct. In the latter sense, we would like to point out that plunder needs to reach a certain level of seriousness in order for this Tribunal to have jurisdiction, as the Trial Chamber in the legal part of the judgement pointed out in paragraph 55. This coupled with the aggravating factors of the systematic plunder and the personal involvement leads us to the conclusion that the sentence of two and a half years is manifestly inadequate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this concluding your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it concludes our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Is there any ...? I don't believe any further question. We -- so this concludes the -- the Prosecution -- the consideration of the Prosecution appeal. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would simply like to apologise once again for disrupting these proceedings and being late. We apologise, and we are indeed very sorry. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we can adjourn now, and we continue tomorrow morning at 8.30 to hear the appeal from Mr. Hadzihasanovic.
